title: Wirtz v. Baldor Electric Co. (1963)
summary: An agency that must decide on the record after a hearing cannot rest its decision on summary tables drawn from confidential survey data it refuses to disclose, once the opposing party has impeached the survey and the agency offers nothing to rehabilitate it.
notes:
Key line: "The Government, in situations of the present sort, has an option: it can hold back confidential material, and take the risk of not being able to prove its case, or it can produce the material and allow it to be the subject of direct and cross-examination." (Washington, J.)

Citation: 337 F.2d 518 (D.C. Cir. 1963).

sections.Parties: The appellant was W. Willard Wirtz, Secretary of Labor, who had determined the prevailing minimum wage in the electrical motors and generators industry under the Walsh Healey Public Contracts Act. The appellees were Baldor Electric Company and other manufacturers of electric motors and generators, who had sued on behalf of themselves and all similarly situated manufacturers. Their trade association, the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, had participated in the administrative hearing and sought the underlying survey data there. The Bureau of Labor Statistics, a part of the Department of Labor, had conducted the wage survey on which the Secretary relied.
sections.Material Facts: The Walsh Healey Act requires government supply contracts to stipulate that the contractor will pay not less than the prevailing minimum wage determined by the Secretary. The 1952 Fulbright Amendment required wage determinations to be made on the record after opportunity for a hearing under the Administrative Procedure Act and gave judicial review to any person adversely affected. To fix minimum wages in the fractional and integral horsepower branches of the industry, the Bureau of Labor Statistics sent a confidential questionnaire to 775 establishments and tabulated wage data for 216 firms. NEMA received the six summary tables five weeks before the hearing, collected answers from 61 companies, and found discrepancies. The hearing examiner refused a subpoena for the questionnaires and the list of establishments, and the Secretary upheld him. Eight conceded errors lowered the tabulated minimums by three and four cents. The Secretary fixed minimums of $1.45 and $1.70 an hour, relying solely on the tables.
sections.Procedural History: The manufacturers sued in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia under section 10 of the Walsh Healey Act and the review provisions of the APA to set aside the Secretary's determination. The district court set the determination aside and enjoined it. The Secretary appealed to the Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which heard argument on June 27, 1963, before Chief Judge Bazelon and Judges Washington and Wright. On December 31, 1963, the court held the determination invalid but remanded the record for findings on which plaintiffs had standing, retaining jurisdiction and staying the injunction. After remand the court issued a per curiam supplemental opinion on June 29, 1964, upholding the standing of five companies, rejecting the Secretary's proposals to supplement the record, and ordering the determination struck down.
sections.Issue: Whether the Secretary could base a prevailing minimum wage determination, which the Fulbright Amendment required to be made on the record after a hearing subject to section 7(c) of the APA, on summary tabulations compiled from confidential survey responses when he refused to disclose the responses or even the names of the establishments surveyed, and when the industry introduced uncontradicted evidence casting serious doubt on the survey's accuracy. The court also decided which manufacturers had standing as persons adversely affected or aggrieved and whether relief should run to the whole industry.
sections.Holding: The court held that admitting the wage tabulations compiled from undisclosed confidential data, which the court would not compel the Secretary to disclose, failed to give the manufacturers the opportunity for rebuttal and cross examination that Congress prescribed. It further held that the determination was not supported by reliable, probative and substantial evidence, because the manufacturers had impeached the survey with probative evidence and the Secretary offered nothing to substantiate the underlying data. Only manufacturers actually paying less than the determined minimum and seeking government contracts had standing, but if any plaintiff had standing the determination should be enjoined for the entire industry. The determination was struck down.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Washington started from section 7(c) of the APA, which placed the burden of proof on the Secretary and gave every party the right to submit rebuttal evidence and conduct such cross examination as may be required for a full and true disclosure of the facts. Summary tables are admissible, but the general rule, illustrated by Powhatan Mining Co. v. Ickes, is that the documents behind them must be introduced or made available so far as needed for rebuttal and cross examination. The court sympathized with the Secretary's fear that disclosure would destroy the Bureau's ability to gather data, but found nothing in the Walsh Healey Act, the Fulbright Amendment or the APA that let a court release him from the procedural commands of the statutes, and cases such as Greene v. McElroy, Jencks and Roviaro pointed toward disclosure of evidence used against a citizen. The court would not itself order the confidential files produced; instead the government had to choose between withholding the material and risking failure of proof, or producing it for examination. Because NEMA's limited survey had turned up eight conceded errors and the Secretary's own witnesses admitted the definition of covered workers was flawed, the tabulations needed reliable supporting evidence, and none was offered. On remedy, a quasi legislative wage rule struck down for one bidder had to fall for all, or the plaintiffs would gain an unconscionable bargaining advantage in lowest bidder competition.

topics.lrs-o-rulemaking-record: Formal procedure required access to individual survey responses so parties could contest the evidence supporting the wage determination.

learning.separateOpinions: None. The panel of Chief Judge Bazelon and Judges Washington and Wright was unanimous, and the supplemental opinion after remand was per curiam. The supplemental opinion rejected the Secretary's proposals to gather 1964 wage data under a renewed pledge of confidentiality, reasoning that 1964 wages could not support a 1960 determination and that a procedure giving not even a modicum of disclosure could not supply the cross examination the statute required.
